newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW -- UK May/June trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- UK May/June trade data.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to data showing a UK May global trade deficit of 508 million stg and a June non-EU trade deficit of 713 million.

"Overall the numbers seem slightly better than the markets had been anticipating. Exports are holding up surprisingly well given the strength of sterling. Equally, there seems to be little evidence that import penetration is rising."

"A fairly mixed bag, with the global balance coming in lower than expected, but we are starting to see pressure on the non-EU trade balance -- exports down 1.4 percent, imports up 0.5 percent. We are likely to see this trend continuing of falling export volumes and rising import volumes in the coming months and that should really offset the value effects that we've seen supporting the trade account earlier in the year. So deteriorating trade accounts should be expected to continue later in the year. Sterling is certainly starting to take its toll. I don't think we've seen much of an impact yet, I think it's going to get a lot worse later in the year."

"The global trade gap in May was much smaller than expected. The narrowing to 508 million stg from a revised 989 million is likely to be taken well by the pound. However, the breakdown is less optimistic, with both exports and imports falling. Although the ONS maintain there is no clear evidence of the currency's climb impacting exports, a 2.6 percent decline was more than anticipated. Meantime, nominal imports will have been held down by the effect of the pound's rise on import prices. The June non-EU data also showed exports continuing to fall and produced a larger deficit than expected. Data not a problem for the pound at this stage since interest rate differentials should ensure comfortable financing of the trade deficit and invisibles are in large surplus anyway. Nonetheless, recent figures do offer some support to industry claims that competitiveness losses are beginning to hurt.
